blocks.intro: Where the water shows up points to the cause:

Water dripping from the ceiling or a wall is a plumbing leak or a [burst pipe](/columbus/burst-pipe-repair). Shut off the main.

blocks.h2: Basement Flooding in Columbus Homes
blocks.intro: Columbus basements face two kinds of water, and the fix depends on which one you have.

items.body: Downtown, Victorian Village and German Village have combined sewers, so heavy rain and sewage share the same pipe. When it fills, water can back up through basement drains.
Across the rest of the city, rainwater gets into cracked laterals and leaky joints. The lateral is the homeowner's responsibility in Columbus, so a camera check is the first step.

The city treats yard grading and drainage as the property owner's responsibility. Water that pools against the house usually ends up in the basement. A clear [catch basin](/columbus/catch-basin) or yard drain helps.

blocks.h2: Basement Waterproofing
bodies: Waterproofing is the right fix when groundwater is coming through the foundation, not up through a drain. Look for damp walls, water along the joint where the wall meets the floor, white chalky deposits and puddles after rain with no drain backing up.

In Central Ohio clay, interior drainage paired with a [sump pump](/columbus/sump-pumps) is the usual answer: the drain tile collects the water and the pump sends it outside. Before recommending anything, we confirm the water isn't a leak or a sewer backup, so you don't pay to fix the wrong problem.

items.q: Who should I call first when my Columbus basement floods?
items.preview: A plumber first, to stop the source. Restoration comes after.
items.answer: A plumber first. If water is still coming in, cleanup won't hold. We find the source and stop it, then a restoration company can dry and clean the space.

items.q: Why does my basement only get water in heavy rain?
items.preview: Either the soil is saturated and groundwater is pushing in, or the sewer is overloaded.
items.answer: In heavy rain, clay soil around the foundation saturates and groundwater pushes in at the walls and floor. At the same time, sewers fill up, especially in combined sewer neighborhoods, and water can come up through the floor drain. We'll tell you which one is happening in your basement.

items.q: What's the difference between a sump pump and an ejector pump?
items.preview: A sump pump removes groundwater. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures up to the sewer.
items.answer: A [sump pump](/columbus/sump-pumps) removes groundwater. It sits in a pit at the lowest point of the basement and pumps water out of the house. An [ejector pump](/columbus/ejector-pump) moves wastewater from fixtures below the main sewer line, like a basement bathroom or laundry room, up to the main sewer level.

items.q: Does homeowners insurance cover basement flooding?
items.preview: Often not for groundwater or sewer backup. Check your policy. We document the cause for your claim.
items.answer: Standard homeowners insurance typically does not cover flooding caused by groundwater, sewer backup or heavy rain. Those events usually require separate flood insurance or a sewer backup rider. If the flooding is caused by a sudden plumbing failure, like a burst pipe, your standard policy may cover it. Check your policy or contact your insurer to confirm. Our technician will document the cause, which may support your claim.

blocks.intro: Columbus winters aren't the coldest in the Midwest, but they swing hard between deep freezes and quick thaws. That swing is what splits pipes.

About 1 in 4 Columbus homes was built before 1960. Galvanized and older copper lines are thinner after decades, so a freeze is more likely to split them.

blocks.h2: What Does a Catch Basin Do?
blocks.body: A catch basin is a box buried at a low point in the yard or driveway, with a grate on top and a pipe leading out. Water flows in, sand and leaves settle to the bottom, and the water leaves through the outlet. Once the bottom fills up, debris reaches the outlet and the water stops leaving. We clean the basin, clear the outlet pipe and repair basins that have cracked, shifted or sunk.

img.alt: Diagram of a catch basin showing the inlet grate, water line, sediment settling in the sump and the outlet pipe carrying water away

blocks.h2: Signs Your Catch Basin Needs Service
blocks.intro: Catch basin trouble shows up as water where it shouldn't be:

tiles.body: If water sits around the grate for hours, the basin or outlet is blocked.
A full basin sends yard water back toward the house, where Central Ohio clay soil holds it against the wall.

tiles.h3: Leaves and Silt on the Grate
tiles.body: If you can see debris piled at the grate, the basin below is likely full.
Ground settling around the basin points to a cracked or collapsing box or outlet pipe.

blocks.h2: What Does an Ejector Pump Do?
blocks.body: Gravity carries most of your home's wastewater to the sewer. A basement bathroom, laundry or bar sink often sits too low for that, so its drains run into a sealed basin in the floor instead. When the basin fills to a set level, a float switches on the ejector pump, and it pushes the wastewater up and into the main sewer line. It looks a lot like a [sump pump](/columbus/sump-pumps), but a sump pump moves groundwater. An ejector pump moves sewage.

img.alt: J. Blanton plumber working on the discharge pipe of a basement sump pump

blocks.h2: Signs Your Ejector Pump Is Failing
blocks.intro: Catch these before the basin overflows:

tiles.body: Stop using every basement fixture and call. The pump isn't keeping up.
A sealed basin shouldn't smell. Odor means a bad seal, a vent problem or a basin that isn't emptying.
If the basement toilet or shower backs up while upstairs drains are fine, start with the pump.
A pump that grinds or never shuts off is fighting a stuck float, a failed check valve or a worn motor.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pumps in Columbus Homes
blocks.intro: Columbus has a lot of basements, and plenty of them have been finished over the years with bathrooms, laundry rooms and bars.

items.h3: The Pump Behind an Overhead Sewer
items.body: An [overhead sewer system](/columbus/overhead-sewer-systems) sends every basement drain to an ejector pit. In combined sewer neighborhoods, that pump is what keeps storm backups out.
Wipes, paper towels and grease. They wrap the impeller and burn out the motor. Toilet paper and wastewater only.

blocks.h2: What Is Hydro Jetting?
blocks.body: Hydro jetting clears a sewer line with a high-pressure water stream, fed through the same cleanout access point used for rodding. A specialized nozzle sprays water in every direction as it moves through the pipe, scouring grease, scale, and roots off the entire pipe wall instead of just cutting a path through the middle. It's the fix for buildup that keeps coming back after rodding, or for roots that have worked into the pipe joints. Rodding opens the line back up. Hydro jetting cleans it.

img.alt: Diagram showing how hydro jetting clears a residential sewer line, with a cross-section view of the underground pipe, jet nozzle, high-pressure water spray, and debris being flushed toward the street connection

blocks.h2: When Your Plumbing Needs Hydro Jetting
blocks.intro: Rodding opens a line. Jetting cleans it. Here's when the second one makes sense:

tiles.body: Grease hardens in layers on the pipe wall. A cable punches through, but the next clog catches on what's left.
A rod leaves root stubs at every joint. Jetting cuts them off flush with the pipe wall.
A lateral has to be clean before it can be lined. We jet it first so the liner seats properly.

tiles.h3: The Clog Keeps Coming Back After Rodding
tiles.body: Rodding breaks through the immediate blockage, but it leaves buildup on the pipe walls that the next clog catches on.

blocks.h2: Why Columbus Lines Need Hydro Jetting
blocks.intro: Columbus asks homeowners and restaurants alike to keep grease out of the sewer, because it builds up, cuts the pipe's capacity and causes backups into homes. Add older clay laterals, and you have the two jobs jetting does best.

items.body: Older homes often have long, flat kitchen drain runs with few cleanouts. Grease settles there first, and jetting is the cleanest way to strip it out.

In neighborhoods built before 1960, clay laterals with open joints let roots in. Jetting clears them out completely, and a [camera inspection](/columbus/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows where they're getting in.

Pressure can hurt a pipe that's already broken, so we camera the lateral before jetting. If a section is cracked or offset, we'll suggest [rodding](/columbus/sewer-rodding) or a [repair](/columbus/sewer-repair) instead.

items.q: Is hydro jetting safe for an older clay sewer line in Columbus?
items.preview: Yes, when the line is checked first. We camera every line before jetting.
items.answer: Yes, when we look first. About 1 in 8 Columbus homes was built before 1940, and many older laterals are clay. We camera the whole line before any jetting, and if a section can't handle the pressure, we won't jet it. We'll show you the footage and suggest another option.

items.q: Can hydro jetting fix a grease problem for good?
items.preview: It clears the grease completely. Keeping it out of the drain keeps it from coming back.
items.answer: Jetting strips grease off the pipe wall completely, so the line flows like it should. Keeping it that way depends on what goes down the drain. Cooking grease should go in the trash after it cools, not down the sink.

items.q: Is hydrojetting better than snaking?
items.preview: It depends on the problem. Snaking is fast and effective for most clogs; hydro jetting is the stronger fix for hardened buildup or root intrusion.
items.answer: It depends on the problem. A drain snake breaks through a clog to restore flow. It's fast, effective, and the right call for most drain issues. Hydro jetting uses high-pressure water to scour the pipe wall clean from the inside. When buildup has hardened on the pipe wall, roots have worked into the joints, or the same clog keeps coming back after rodding, hydro jetting is the stronger fix. A camera inspection tells us which one your line actually needs.

items.q: How much does hydro jetting cost in Columbus?
items.preview: It depends on line length, buildup and what the camera finds. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on how long the line is, how heavy the buildup is and what the camera shows. Older clay lines with heavy roots can take more work. We show you what's in the pipe and give you a flat price before any work begins.

items.q: Can hydrojetting destroy roots?
items.preview: It clears roots that have already worked into the line, but it can't stop new roots from growing back.
items.answer: It can cut through and flush out roots that have worked their way into pipe joints, clearing the line completely. What it can't do is stop roots from growing back. That requires repairing or relining the pipe where the intrusion is happening. The camera inspection shows exactly where the roots are entering so you know what you're dealing with before you decide.

tiles.h3: A Clean Line That Still Backs Up

tiles.body: Sewage in a finished basement once is enough. Another temporary fix isn't worth round two.

blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: In most basements, the floor drain, basement toilet and laundry drain by gravity into a sewer line that leaves the house below the floor. When the sewer outside fills up in a storm, water can flow right back up that path. An overhead system cuts that path off. Those low drains empty into a sealed pit, an [ejector pump](/columbus/ejector-pump) lifts the wastewater up to a new line near the basement ceiling, and a check valve keeps it from falling back. From there it flows to the sewer by gravity, just like your upstairs drains.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewers and Columbus Basements
blocks.intro: Overhead sewers make the most sense in the parts of Columbus where storms hit the sewers hardest.

items.body: Downtown, Victorian Village and German Village have combined sewers, where stormwater and sewage share one pipe. In heavy rain, that pipe can fill to the level of a basement drain.

items.h3: Older Laterals That Let Rain In
items.body: Across older parts of the city, rainwater gets into cracked laterals and joints. We camera your lateral first, because sometimes a repair is the fix, not a conversion.
Every fixture in the basement is a way in for a backup. An overhead system routes all of them to a sealed pit, and an [ejector pump](/columbus/ejector-pump) lifts the wastewater up and out.

blocks.body: Sewer rodding clears a blocked main line with a long, flexible steel cable fed through a cleanout access point. blocks.h2: What Is Trenchless Sewer Repair?
blocks.body: Trenchless sewer repair, also called no-dig sewer repair, fixes a damaged pipe without digging a trench along its full length. Instead of opening up your yard from the house to the street, we work through one or two access points and repair the pipe from the inside or replace it in place. There are two main methods: cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) lining and pipe bursting. Both fix the line underground, so what's above it stays untouched.

img.alt: Two J. Blanton plumbers setting up sewer camera and cable equipment beside a home's foundation before a trenchless sewer repair

blocks.h2: Why Trenchless Fits Columbus Homes
blocks.intro: In Columbus, the homeowner is responsible for the lateral, and that includes restoring whatever gets dug up to reach it. On many older lots, that's a lot.

items.body: In German Village, Victorian Village and other older neighborhoods, laterals run under brick sidewalks, narrow side yards and garden beds. Working underground leaves them alone.

items.h3: Mature Trees in Clintonville and Upper Arlington
items.body: Big old trees and old clay laterals tend to share the same ground. A trench cuts through the roots you want to keep. Lining doesn't.
Root-cracked joints, minor offsets and aging clay are what lining handles best. A liner seals every joint at once, so roots have nowhere to get back in.
Any digging starts with a call to OUPS (Ohio811) to mark buried gas, electric and water lines. Trenchless keeps the digging to one or two small pits.

blocks.h2: When Does Trenchless Apply?
blocks.intro: Backups, slow drains, sewer odor, soft or unusually lush patches of grass, and gurgling drains are the most common signs of a damaged sewer line. Which repair method fits comes down to the type and extent of the damage.
head: Situation

blocks.note: Not sure which category applies to your line? A [camera inspection](/columbus/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows exactly what's happening underground before any repair method gets recommended.

blocks.h2: How Trenchless Sewer Repair Works in Columbus
blocks.intro: Both methods replace a trench. The camera decides which one fits your lateral.

steps.body: We clean the line, pull a resin-coated liner through it and cure it in place, creating a seamless new pipe inside the old one. Our trucks use light-cured lining, which cures faster than older steam or water methods.
When the old pipe is too broken to line, we pull a new pipe through it while breaking the old one apart around it. The lateral is replaced without a trench.
We record the line before we recommend a method and again when we're done, and you get a flat rate before any work starts.

blocks.h2: Signs Your Water Heater Needs Repair
blocks.intro: Most heaters warn you before they quit. These are the calls we get most in Columbus:

tiles.body: Minerals from the water settle as sediment on the bottom of the tank. The burner heats through it and it crackles. It's a sign the tank needs flushing.
Sediment takes up room in the tank, or a burner or element isn't heating fully.
A drip at the drain valve or relief valve is usually a repair. A leak from the tank body means the tank has failed.
Rust-colored water or a rotten-egg smell at the hot tap points to a corroding tank or a worn anode rod.

blocks.h2: Water Heater Problems in Columbus Homes
blocks.intro: Columbus water comes from three treatment plants, and its hardness depends on which one serves your neighborhood. In 2025, the averages ran from 98 to 125 milligrams per liter.

items.body: Hard water leaves minerals behind every time the tank heats. Over years, that layer makes the heater work harder, adds noise and shortens its life. Flushing is the simple fix.

bodies: Flushing drains the sediment that settles at the bottom of the tank. In Columbus, where the water is moderately hard to hard, that sediment builds steadily. We also check the anode rod, which protects the tank from corrosion, plus the relief valve and the burner or elements.

Most manufacturers suggest flushing a tank about once a year. Tankless units need regular descaling instead. If your heater has never been flushed, start with a maintenance visit before deciding it needs replacing.
